opus-5.5.text:
I think the interaction is going to shift quite fundamentally. Today most people still interact with AI in a very synchronous way: you type a question, you wait a few seconds, you get an answer, and then you type again. That made sense when the model could only handle short, single-step tasks. But as models get stronger, especially in reasoning and in using tools over long horizons, that turn-by-turn chat starts to become a bottleneck.

What I expect is a move from synchronous to asynchronous interaction. You give the agent a goal, maybe a fairly vague one, and it goes off and works for minutes, hours, eventually maybe days. It searches, writes code, runs experiments, checks its own results, and comes back to you with something close to a finished product rather than a single reply. So the human's role changes from operator to something more like a manager or a reviewer. You set direction, you give feedback at key checkpoints, and you judge the output.

That also changes what a good interface looks like. Instead of a chat box, you might need something closer to a workspace, where you can see what the agent is doing, intervene when it goes in the wrong direction, and hand off many tasks in parallel. The bandwidth between human and AI goes up, not because you type more, but because each instruction carries much more leverage.

There's a deeper point too. The more capable the model is, the less you should need to specify how to do something. Early on, people wrote very detailed prompts and workflows because the model needed that scaffolding. As capability improves, a lot of that scaffolding gets absorbed into the model itself. So the interaction becomes simpler on the surface, more about intent and taste, while the complexity moves underneath into the agent's own planning.

And honestly, I think we're still early. Many of the interaction forms that will feel natural in a few years probably haven't been invented yet. Things like how you build trust with an agent that runs for a long time, or how multiple agents and multiple people collaborate on the same task. Those are open questions, and I think whoever figures out the right form factor alongside the model capability will have a big advantage.

r001.rationale: The response says users may watch what the agent is doing and intervene at checkpoints, but it does not clearly identify inspecting intermediate results during step-by-step execution.

r002.rationale: It explicitly links stronger model capabilities to a shift from turn-by-turn chat toward asynchronous, goal-directed interaction.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the interaction method is actually going to become less of a thing, not more. Right now a lot of the product work around agents is about the interface: the chat box, the canvas, the sidebar, how you approve each step. That's necessary today because the model isn't capable enough to be trusted on its own, so you build all this scaffolding for the human to stay in the loop and correct it.

But if you look at the trend, as the model gets more capable, the amount of interaction you need per unit of work goes down. You give it a goal, it runs for an hour, maybe for a day, and it comes back with a result. The interface becomes more like how you'd work with a strong colleague. You don't tell a good engineer which file to open. You tell them the problem, and you check in occasionally.

So I'd say two things change. First, the granularity of interaction shifts from actions to intentions. Instead of "click here, edit this," it's "here's what I want, here are the constraints." Second, the interaction becomes more asynchronous. The model does long-horizon work in the background and surfaces only when something actually needs your judgment, or when it's done.

The interesting question is what the model needs from the human in that world. I think it's mostly context and taste. The human's job is to say what matters, what good looks like, and what the hard constraints are. Everything else should ideally be handled by the model itself, and if it can't be, that's a capability gap, not something you should fix with a better UI.

And I'd add that from our perspective, as a model company, we try not to overdesign interaction around today's limitations. If you build a very elaborate interface for a model that needs correcting every three steps, that interface becomes obsolete the moment the model stops needing it. So we'd rather push on the model side, on long-horizon agentic capability, and let the interaction simplify as a consequence.

r001.rationale: It describes approving each step and keeping the human in the loop to correct the agent, communicating review of intermediate steps as interaction.

r002.rationale: It says that as models become more capable, interaction per unit of work decreases and shifts toward intentions and asynchronous check-ins.

astra-6.text:
I think the interaction will gradually shift from giving detailed instructions to expressing an intention. Today, you often have to break a task into steps for the model and check each result. As models become more capable, you should be able to describe what you want to achieve, give the relevant constraints, and let the agent figure out how to get there.

That also changes the interface. A chat window is useful, but it may not be sufficient for work that takes a long time or involves many decisions. You might want to see the agent’s progress, inspect something it produced, or intervene at an important point without having to follow every step.

So I don’t think better agents necessarily mean more conversation. They could mean less conversation, but more meaningful interaction. The agent needs to know when it can proceed independently and when asking you a question would actually improve the outcome. Getting that balance right is a big part of making these systems useful.

r001.rationale: The response describes breaking a task into steps and checking each result, and also mentions inspecting what the agent produced.

r002.rationale: It says that as models become more capable, interaction shifts from detailed instructions toward expressing an intention and letting the agent proceed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interaction will gradually shift from giving instructions at every step to describing a goal and letting the agent figure out how to achieve it. Today, you often have to provide a lot of context, break the task down, and check the result repeatedly. As models become more capable, they should be able to take on more of that work themselves.

But that doesn’t necessarily mean everything becomes a chat interface. For some tasks, conversation is natural. For others, you want to see a document, a visual interface, or the progress of a task. The agent should choose a useful way to present its work, and you should be able to intervene when needed.

So the key question becomes when the agent should act independently and when it should come back to you. A good agent can handle the details while still asking you about decisions that depend on your preferences. That balance is probably more important than any particular interface.

r001.rationale: It describes breaking a task into steps and repeatedly checking results, identifying iterative result inspection during task execution as part of the interaction.

r002.rationale: It says that as models become more capable, interaction shifts toward giving a goal and letting agents handle more of the work.
